etymology: From crucify (Latin crucifigere, to fasten to a cross) and flesh (the fallen nature, Greek sarx); the believer’s mortifying of sinful desires.
biblical_def: To crucify the flesh is the believer’s lifelong putting to death of the sinful nature and its desires, by the Spirit, as a fruit and duty of union with Christ. Paul writes that “they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.” In one sense this crucifixion is already accomplished in the believer’s union with the crucified Christ: our old man is crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, and the believer is to reckon himself dead indeed unto sin. In another sense it is a daily duty, the ongoing work of mortification: “if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.” The figure of crucifixion is exact and severe—it is not the taming of the flesh, nor a truce with it, but its execution; a slow, painful, certain putting to death, as a man nailed to a cross dies by degrees yet surely. This work is not done in the believer’s own strength but by the indwelling Spirit, and it is not optional but the mark of those who belong to Christ. The dictionary holds the crucifying of the flesh as the negative side of sanctification, the inseparable companion of living unto God: the believer does not merely add new virtues but slays old sins, making no provision for the flesh, and reckoning the cross to be the death of his corruption as well as the ground of his pardon.
webster_summary: The believer’s lifelong putting to death of the sinful nature and its desires by the Spirit—the severe figure of execution, not truce—the negative side of sanctification.
webster_full: CRUCIFY THE FLESH, the believer’s mortifying of the sinful nature.
“They that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.”
Accomplished already in union with the crucified Christ; the old man crucified with Him.
A daily duty: “mortify the deeds of the body” through the Spirit.
Not a truce with sin but its execution—a certain putting to death.
scriptures: Gal 5:24
And they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
Rom 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
Rom 6:6
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
corruption_summary: Mortification is softened into self-improvement or self-acceptance, and the war against indwelling sin is abandoned.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the severity of the figure: the flesh is to be crucified, not coddled, managed, or merely improved. The therapy-culture of self-acceptance counsels the believer to embrace his desires and make peace with himself; Scripture commands him to put those sinful desires to death. As the Puritan Owen warned, be killing sin or it will be killing you; there is no neutrality and no truce in this war.

A second corruption severs mortification from the Spirit and from union with Christ, turning it into mere willpower and self-denial—a religion of gritted teeth that breeds either pride or despair. The dictionary holds the true doctrine: the believer crucifies the flesh by the Spirit, on the ground of being already crucified with Christ, reckoning himself dead to sin and alive unto God. The killing of sin is real, daily, and painful, but it is the work of grace in the soul, not the soul’s unaided struggle; and it is the certain mark of all who are Christ’s.
roots_summary: The phrase applies the cross to the sinful nature, naming the believer’s daily execution of indwelling sin by the Spirit.
roots_lines: Greek stauroō — to crucify; here applied to the flesh and its lusts.
Greek sarx — flesh, the fallen sinful nature with its desires.
Greek thanatoō — to put to death; “mortify the deeds of the body.”
The “old man” — the unregenerate self, crucified with Christ.
Mortification is the negative side of sanctification, paired with vivification.
usage: Crucifying the flesh is preached as the believer’s daily duty of mortification.
Owen’s “be killing sin or it will be killing you” summarizes the doctrine.
It is set against self-acceptance and against mere willpower severed from the Spirit.

etymology: From prevail (Latin praevalere, to be stronger, to have power) and prayer; prayer that obtains its request by the power of God.
biblical_def: Prevailing prayer is earnest, persevering, believing prayer that lays hold of God and obtains the blessing—not by wearing down a reluctant God, but by pleading His promises in dependence on His will. The Scripture is full of such prayer. Jacob wrestled with the angel and would not let him go until he was blessed, and as a prince he had power with God and with men and prevailed, whence he was named Israel. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much: Elijah, a man of like passions, prayed earnestly that it might not rain, and it rained not; and he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain. The Lord Jesus taught His disciples that men ought always to pray and not to faint, in the parable of the importunate widow and of the friend at midnight, urging persistence; and He bade them ask, seek, and knock, with the promise that the asking soul receives. Prevailing prayer is marked by importunity that will not give up, by faith that rests on God’s word and character, by submission to His sovereign will, and by praying in the name of Christ. It does not move God to do what is against His purpose; rather, God ordains the prayers of His people as the appointed means by which He brings His purposes to pass. The dictionary commends prevailing prayer as the believer’s wrestling privilege: to plead with God boldly and persistently, on the warrant of His promises, until the blessing comes.
webster_summary: Earnest, persevering, believing prayer that lays hold of God and obtains the blessing by pleading His promises in submission to His will—the wrestling of Jacob, the importunity Christ urged.
webster_full: PREVAILING PRAYER, earnest, persevering, believing prayer that obtains the blessing.
Not wearing down a reluctant God, but pleading His promises in dependence on His will.
Pictured in Jacob, who wrestled and would not let go until he was blessed.
“The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.”
Christ taught that men ought always to pray and not to faint.
scriptures: And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.
Jas 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
Luk 18:1
And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;
Mat 7:7
Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:
corruption_summary: Prevailing prayer is distorted into a technique that compels God, or dismissed altogether as if persistence were faithless.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the balance of boldness and submission. Prevailing prayer is importunate and persevering—it wrestles like Jacob and will not let go—yet it always bows to the sovereign will of God, praying as the Lord prayed, “not my will, but thine, be done.” It does not bend God to the creature’s purpose but pleads God’s own promises and rests in His wisdom.

A corruption on one side turns prevailing prayer into a technique or formula that supposedly compels God to grant whatever is named in enough faith—the error of the word-of-faith and prosperity teaching, which makes the creature sovereign and God the servant. A corruption on the other side dismisses persistence as faithless, as though to ask twice were to doubt. Scripture refutes both: God ordains importunate prayer as the means of His blessing, commands His people to pray and not to faint, and grants in His own time and way what is according to His will. The dictionary commends bold, persevering, submissive prayer as the wrestling privilege of the saints.
roots_summary: The phrase names prayer that has power with God, pleading His promises with importunity until the blessing comes.
roots_lines: Hebrew sārāh — to strive, contend; Jacob “had power with God” and prevailed.
Greek energeō — to be effectual, to work powerfully; the “effectual fervent prayer.”
Greek anaideia — importunity, shameless persistence; the friend at midnight.
Prevailing prayer pleads God’s promises, not the creature’s will.
It is offered in the name of Christ, the appointed ground of access.
usage: Jacob’s wrestling at Peniel is the classic image of prevailing prayer.
Christ’s parables of the importunate widow and friend at midnight teach persistence.
It is balanced against word-of-faith techniques that claim to compel God.

etymology: From doer (one who performs) and the Word (the Scripture, the revealed will of God); James’s charge to obey, not merely hear.
biblical_def: A doer of the word is one who not only hears the Scripture but obeys it, putting it into practice in his life. The phrase comes from the Epistle of James, which presses the point with great force: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” James likens the hearer who does not obey to a man beholding his natural face in a glass, who goes his way and straightway forgets what manner of man he was; but the doer, who looks into the perfect law of liberty and continues therein, is not a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, and shall be blessed in his deed. The doctrine is not works-righteousness—James does not teach that obedience earns salvation—but the necessary fruit and evidence of a living faith, for faith without works is dead. The same Lord who said “Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” built His Sermon on the Mount to this conclusion: the wise man hears His sayings and does them, building on the rock, while the foolish hears and does them not, building on the sand. The dictionary holds the doctrine of the doer of the word as the test of genuine religion: hearing, even delighting in, the Word is not enough; saving faith works, obeys, and bears fruit, and the profession that does not issue in obedience is self-deception. The proof of having truly heard is doing.
webster_summary: One who obeys the Scripture, not merely hears it—James’s charge to be doers of the word and not hearers only; obedience the necessary fruit and evidence of living faith.
webster_full: DOER OF THE WORD, one who obeys the Scripture, not merely hears it.
“Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.”
The hearer who forgets is like a man who beholds his face in a glass and forgets it.
Not works-righteousness, but the necessary fruit and evidence of living faith.
Christ’s wise man hears His sayings and does them, building on the rock.
scriptures: Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Jas 1:25
But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.
Luk 6:46
And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?
Mat 7:24
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
corruption_summary: Hearing and approving the Word is mistaken for obeying it, and a fruitless profession is treated as living faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that hearing is not obeying. An age rich in sermons, books, podcasts, and conferences may grow vast in religious information while remaining barren of obedience—hearers only, deceiving their own selves. James and the Lord Jesus alike press the test: the proof of having heard is doing, and the profession that bears no fruit of obedience is dead and self-deceived.

The doctrine must be guarded on both sides. It is not works-righteousness; the doer is not justified by his doing, for justification is by faith alone. But the faith that justifies is never alone—it works, obeys, and bears fruit. To press obedience as the fruit and evidence of faith is not to deny grace but to honor it, for grace produces a changed and obedient life. The dictionary holds the doer of the word against both the antinomian who divorces faith from obedience and the legalist who makes obedience the ground of acceptance: faith alone justifies, but obedient doing proves the faith to be alive.
roots_summary: The phrase names the obedient hearer, whose doing of the Word proves the reality of his faith.
roots_lines: Greek poiētēs — a doer, maker, performer; “doers of the word.”
Greek akroatēs — a hearer; the merely passive listener James warns against.
Greek logos — word; the Scripture, the revealed will of God.
The “perfect law of liberty” — the gospel law into which the doer looks and continues.
The doing is fruit and evidence of faith, not the ground of justification.
usage: “Doers of the word, and not hearers only” is preached against sermon-rich but fruitless religion.
It is balanced to teach obedience as evidence, not ground, of justification.
Christ’s wise and foolish builders illustrate hearing-and-doing versus hearing-only.

etymology: From liberty (Latin libertas, freedom) and Christ; the spiritual freedom the gospel gives the believer.
biblical_def: Liberty in Christ is the spiritual freedom the gospel gives the believer—freedom from the guilt and dominion of sin, from the curse and condemnation of the law, from the bondage of Satan and death, and from the rigor of the ceremonial yoke. “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.” This liberty is not freedom to sin but freedom from sin: the believer is freed from sin’s reign that he might become the servant of righteousness and of God. The truth makes him free, and if the Son makes him free, he is free indeed. Christian liberty also includes freedom of conscience, which is bound by the Word of God alone and not by the commandments of men; in matters that Scripture leaves indifferent, the believer is free, yet must not use his liberty for an occasion to the flesh, nor to wound a weaker brother, but by love serve one another. The dictionary holds liberty in Christ in its full biblical breadth and its careful limits. It is glorious freedom—from condemnation, from sin’s power, from man-made yokes—purchased by the blood of Christ. But it is never license: the same grace that frees from the law as a covenant of works writes the law upon the heart as a rule of life, so that the freed man delights to obey, and his liberty is the liberty of a son, not the lawlessness of a rebel.
webster_summary: The believer’s gospel freedom—from sin’s guilt and dominion, the law’s curse, Satan, and man-made yokes—a freedom from sin unto righteousness, never a license to sin.
webster_full: LIBERTY IN CHRIST, the spiritual freedom the gospel gives the believer.
Freedom from the guilt and dominion of sin and the curse of the law.
“Stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free.”
Not freedom to sin but freedom from sin unto the service of righteousness.
Includes freedom of conscience, bound by the Word of God alone, not the commandments of men.
scriptures: Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Joh 8:36
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
Gal 5:13
For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
As free, and not using your liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, but as the servants of God.
corruption_summary: Christian liberty is twisted into license for the flesh, or denied by a legalism that binds the conscience with man-made rules.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption on one side is the antinomian abuse that turns liberty into license—using the grace of God as a cloak for sin and an occasion to the flesh. But Paul expressly forbids it: the called are free, yet not to indulge the flesh; freedom in Christ is freedom from sin, not freedom to sin. The grace that justifies also sanctifies, and the freed man is the willing servant of righteousness, not a lawless rebel.

The corruption on the other side is legalism, which binds the conscience with commandments of men and adds yokes Christ never imposed—the very bondage Galatians fights. The dictionary holds the balance the Reformed confessions teach: the conscience is free, bound by God’s Word alone; the believer is loosed from the ceremonial law and from man-made rules; yet his liberty is governed by love, considerate of the weaker brother, and obedient to the moral law as a rule of life. True Christian liberty is the freedom of a son who delights to do his Father’s will, equally distant from license and from legalism.
roots_summary: The phrase names the gospel freedom of the believer—from sin, law-curse, and man-made yokes—a freedom unto obedience, not license.
roots_lines: Greek eleutheria — freedom, liberty; “the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free.”
Greek zugos — yoke; the “yoke of bondage” not to be taken up again.
Liberty of conscience — bound by the Word of God alone, not the commandments of men.
Freedom from sin’s dominion, not freedom to sin; “the servants of God.”
Governed by love: not an occasion to the flesh, nor a stumbling to the weak.
usage: Liberty in Christ is preached as freedom from sin’s guilt and dominion, not license to sin.
Freedom of conscience is cited against binding believers with man-made rules.
It is held between the antinomian abuse and the legalist denial.

etymology: From new and heart (Hebrew lēb, the inner seat of mind, will, and affections); the regenerated inner man promised in the covenant.
biblical_def: The new heart is the regenerated inner man—the renewed mind, will, and affections—which God gives in the new birth, fulfilling the great covenant promise of the prophets. “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.” By nature the heart is stony, dead, hard, deceitful above all things and desperately wicked, unable and unwilling to love God or obey His law. In regeneration God does what the sinner cannot do for himself: He removes the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh, writes His law within, and puts His Spirit in the inner man, so that the renewed person now loves what he once hated and hates what he once loved. This is the work of God alone, sovereign and creative—“create in me a clean heart, O God”—not the sinner’s self-reformation but his re-creation. The new heart does not make the believer perfect in this life, for sin remains and must be mortified, but it is a real, radical, and permanent change of nature, the root from which all true obedience grows. The dictionary holds the new heart as the necessary inward change without which no man can see the kingdom of God: religion that does not flow from a new heart is mere outward conformity, but the regenerate, given a heart of flesh, are made willing in the day of God’s power.
webster_summary: The regenerated inner man—renewed mind, will, and affections—which God sovereignly gives in the new birth, removing the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh.
webster_full: NEW HEART, the regenerated inner man given in the new birth.
The covenant promise: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.”
God removes the stony heart and gives a heart of flesh.
The sovereign, creative work of God, not the sinner’s self-reformation.
The root from which all true obedience grows.
scriptures: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
And I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh:
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
corruption_summary: The new heart is reduced to a decision or a moral resolve, denying that regeneration is the sovereign, creative work of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the new heart is God’s gift, not man’s achievement. “I will give you” and “I will take away” are the promises of a sovereign God who does for the dead sinner what he cannot do for himself. Against the notion that a man may turn over a new leaf, decide for God, or reform himself into a Christian, Scripture sets the radical re-creation of the inner man by the Spirit—a heart of stone removed, a heart of flesh given.

A second corruption mistakes the new heart for mere emotional warmth or a moment of decision, severing it from the lasting change of nature it names. The new heart is not a passing feeling but a permanent renewal of mind, will, and affections, the root of a transformed life. The dictionary holds it as the necessary inward change without which no man can enter the kingdom: not self-improvement but new creation, not the sinner’s decision moving God, but God’s sovereign grace making the unwilling willing and the dead alive.
roots_summary: The phrase names the regenerated inner man, the heart of flesh God gives in fulfilling the new covenant.
roots_lines: Hebrew lēb — heart, the inner seat of mind, will, and affections.
The “heart of stone” — the hard, dead, unregenerate nature.
The “heart of flesh” — the soft, living, responsive heart God gives.
The promise belongs to the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36.
Given sovereignly by God in regeneration, not produced by the sinner’s will.
usage: The new heart is the covenant promise preached on the necessity of regeneration.
Ezekiel’s heart of stone and heart of flesh picture the change God works.
It is set against decisional and self-reform views of conversion.

etymology: From hope (a confident expectation) and salvation; the believer’s assured looking for the consummation of his redemption.
biblical_def: The hope of salvation is the believer’s confident expectation of the full and final completion of his redemption—the resurrection of the body, the day of judgment safely passed, and the everlasting enjoyment of God in glory. Biblical hope is not the wishful uncertainty the world means by the word, but a settled and certain expectation grounded on the promise and faithfulness of God: “hope maketh not ashamed,” for it rests not on the believer’s changeable feelings but on the unchangeable God and the finished work of Christ. Paul names it among the Christian’s armor—“for an helmet, the hope of salvation”—the guard of the mind in spiritual warfare; and he calls it an anchor of the soul, sure and steadfast, entering into that within the veil, fastened to the risen Christ Himself. This hope is the patient expectation of what is not yet seen, for we are saved by hope, and hope that is seen is not hope; and it purifies, for every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself. It is a living hope, begotten by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, reserved in heaven and kept by the power of God. The dictionary holds the hope of salvation as one of the three abiding graces with faith and love: a sure and certain expectation that sustains the believer through suffering, guards his mind, anchors his soul, and purifies his life, until hope gives way to sight and the saved are gathered home.
webster_summary: The believer’s confident, certain expectation of the completion of his redemption—an anchor of the soul and a helmet in warfare, grounded on God’s promise and the risen Christ.
webster_full: HOPE OF SALVATION, the believer’s confident expectation of his completed redemption.
Not wishful uncertainty, but a settled expectation grounded on God’s promise.
“For an helmet, the hope of salvation”—the guard of the mind in warfare.
An anchor of the soul, sure and steadfast, entering within the veil.
A living hope, begotten by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.
scriptures: But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation.
Heb 6:19
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;
Rom 5:5
And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
corruption_summary: Biblical hope is weakened into worldly wishful thinking, or shifted from the world to come onto this present life.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certainty of biblical hope. The world uses “hope” for a wish that may or may not come true; Scripture uses it for a confident expectation grounded on the faithfulness of God and the finished work of Christ. The hope of salvation is an anchor sure and steadfast, not a fragile wish; it maketh not ashamed because it rests on God, not on the believer’s feelings or performance.

A second corruption shifts the believer’s hope from the world to come onto this present life—health, wealth, comfort, and earthly success—as though the gospel’s promise were a better life now rather than glory hereafter. Paul says that if in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable. The dictionary keeps the hope of salvation fixed on its true object: the resurrection of the body, the judgment safely passed, and the everlasting enjoyment of God. This hope sustains the suffering saint, guards his mind, anchors his soul, and purifies his walk until hope is swallowed up in sight.
roots_summary: The phrase names the believer’s certain expectation of completed redemption, an anchor and a helmet grounded on the risen Christ.
roots_lines: Greek elpis — hope, confident expectation, not mere wishing.
Greek ankura — anchor; hope as “an anchor of the soul.”
The helmet image — hope as the guard of the mind in spiritual warfare.
A “lively” (living) hope, begotten by Christ’s resurrection.
One of the three abiding graces: faith, hope, and love.
usage: The hope of salvation is preached as certain expectation, not worldly wishful thinking.
Its anchor and helmet images teach hope’s guarding and steadying power.
It is fixed on the world to come against shifting hope onto this present life.

etymology: From experiential (also experimental, of that which is known by experience) and religion; the older Puritan term for religion truly felt and lived, not merely professed.
biblical_def: Experiential religion—also called experimental religion in the older usage—is true godliness as it is actually known, felt, and lived in the soul, as distinct from a merely notional, formal, or professed Christianity. The older divines spoke of “experimental” faith not in the modern sense of trial-and-error, but in the sense of that which is proved and known by experience: the doctrines of grace not only believed in the head but tasted in the heart. Such religion involves the soul’s real dealings with God—conviction of sin, the felt need of a Saviour, the sweetness of pardon, communion with Christ, the witness of the Spirit, the warfare with indwelling sin, seasons of darkness and of joy, and growing conformity to Christ. It is the religion of the Psalms, where the writer pours out his soul, pants after God, and tastes that the LORD is good. The Puritans and their heirs prized experiential preaching that addresses the varied states of the soul and traces the work of grace within. The dictionary commends experiential religion as the necessary heart of true Christianity, while guarding it on both sides: it is not the cold orthodoxy that holds the truth without ever feeling its power, nor the unstable enthusiasm that trusts feelings without doctrine, but sound doctrine experienced—truth known not only as fact but as life, the Word of God brought home to the soul by the Spirit and proved in the believer’s own walk with God.
webster_summary: True godliness as actually known, felt, and lived in the soul—the Puritan “experimental” religion of sound doctrine experienced, distinct from cold orthodoxy and from doctrineless enthusiasm.
webster_full: EXPERIENTIAL RELIGION, true godliness known, felt, and lived in the soul.
Also “experimental” religion: that which is proved and known by experience.
The doctrines of grace not only believed in the head but tasted in the heart.
The religion of the Psalms—the soul’s real dealings with God.
Guarded on both sides: not cold orthodoxy, nor doctrineless enthusiasm, but doctrine experienced.
scriptures: Psa 34:8
O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
Psa 42:1
As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.
Rom 8:16
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:
corruption_summary: Experience is severed from doctrine and made the test of truth, or religion is reduced to cold orthodoxy with no felt power at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that true religion must be experienced and not merely professed—sound doctrine brought home to the heart by the Spirit and proved in the life. Against a dead orthodoxy that holds the right truths without ever feeling their power, the Psalms and the Puritans summon the soul to taste that the LORD is good, to pant after God, and to know the witness of the Spirit. Truth held only in the head, never tasted in the heart, is barren.

Yet experiential religion is corrupted when experience is cut loose from doctrine and made the judge of truth—the modern error of trusting feelings, impressions, and inner experiences over the written Word. The dictionary holds the older balance: experience is the warming and proving of sound doctrine, never its replacement. The Word of God is the rule; experience is the heart’s real participation in what the Word reveals. A felt religion without doctrine is unstable enthusiasm; a doctrine without felt power is dead formality; experiential religion is the two joined, truth known as life.
roots_summary: The phrase names religion proved by experience—sound doctrine felt and lived, the heart’s real dealings with God.
roots_lines: Latin experientia — experience, knowledge gained by living through a thing.
The older “experimental” — proved by experience, not trial-and-error.
Greek geuomai — to taste; “taste and see that the LORD is good.”
The witness of the Spirit with the believer’s spirit is a chief experiential mark.
Prized in Puritan preaching that traces the work of grace in the soul.
usage: Experiential (experimental) religion is the older term for godliness truly felt and lived.
Puritan experiential preaching addresses the varied states of the soul.
It is held between dead orthodoxy and doctrineless enthusiasm.

etymology: From worldly (of this present age) and sorrow (grief); the false grief Paul contrasts with godly sorrow.
biblical_def: Worldly sorrow is the false and fruitless grief over sin that springs not from love to God but from love to self—the regret of one sorry for the consequences of his sin rather than for the sin itself, which Paul says “worketh death.” The apostle draws the sharp contrast: “For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.” Godly sorrow grieves that God has been offended, hates the sin as sin, and turns the soul to God in genuine repentance that issues in changed life; it produces, as Paul lists, carefulness, indignation against the sin, fear, vehement desire, zeal, and the setting right of wrong. Worldly sorrow, by contrast, mourns only the loss, the shame, the punishment, or the exposure—it weeps over the wages of sin while still loving the sin; it is the remorse of Cain, who feared his punishment, and of Judas, who was filled with remorse and went and hanged himself, but never repented unto life; whereas Peter, with godly sorrow, wept bitterly and was restored. The dictionary holds the distinction as vital to discerning true conversion: many sorrow for sin who are never saved, for their grief is self-centered and barren. Worldly sorrow may look like repentance and even shed many tears, yet it works death; only godly sorrow, grieving that God is dishonored and turning to Him through Christ, works repentance unto salvation.
webster_summary: The false, self-centered grief over sin’s consequences—not over the sin itself—which Paul says worketh death, contrasted with godly sorrow that worketh repentance unto salvation.
webster_full: WORLDLY SORROW, false grief over sin springing from love of self, not love of God.
“The sorrow of the world worketh death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).
Mourns the consequences, shame, or punishment while still loving the sin.
The remorse of Cain and of Judas, who never repented unto life.
Contrasted with godly sorrow, which worketh repentance to salvation.
scriptures: For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Mat 27:3
Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,
And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.

For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge!
corruption_summary: Mere regret over consequences is mistaken for true repentance, and the distinguishing of false from godly sorrow is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul’s sharp distinction between two sorrows that may look alike but lead to opposite ends. Worldly sorrow weeps over the wages of sin—the exposure, the shame, the punishment—while the heart still loves the sin; godly sorrow grieves that God has been offended and turns the soul from sin to God. The one worketh death; the other, repentance unto salvation. A therapy-culture that treats all grief over wrongdoing as equally healing cannot make this distinction; Scripture insists upon it.

The contrast of Judas and Peter makes it plain. Both grieved bitterly over their sin against Christ; but Judas’s sorrow was the despairing remorse of the world, which drove him to the rope, while Peter’s was godly sorrow that wept and returned and was restored. The dictionary holds the difference as a vital test of conversion: many tears are shed in worldly sorrow that never reach repentance. Only the grief that hates sin as against God, and flees to Christ for pardon, works the repentance that is unto life.
roots_summary: The phrase names the false grief over sin’s consequences that works death, set against the godly sorrow that works repentance.
roots_lines: Greek lupē — sorrow, grief; the word for both sorrows in 2 Corinthians 7.
“Of the world,” tou kosmou — springing from this present age and the love of self.
Greek metanoia — repentance, the change of mind godly sorrow works.
Judas’s remorse (metamelomai) is distinguished from saving repentance.
Peter’s bitter weeping is the pattern of godly sorrow restored.
usage: Worldly sorrow is preached as the counterfeit of true repentance.
Judas and Peter are contrasted to distinguish the two sorrows.
It warns that tears over sin’s consequences are not yet repentance unto life.

etymology: From Psalm 34:8, “O taste and see that the LORD is good”; an invitation to know the goodness of God by experience.
biblical_def: “O taste and see that the LORD is good” is the invitation of Psalm 34 to know the goodness of God not by report only but by personal experience—to prove for oneself, in the soul’s own dealings with Him, that the LORD is good and that blessed is the man that trusteth in Him. The figure of tasting is bold and tender: as a man knows the sweetness of honey not by hearing of it but by tasting, so the believer comes to know the goodness of God by trusting Him, fleeing to Him, and finding Him faithful. The verse marries experience to action—tasting is by trusting; the goodness of the LORD is proved in the very act of taking refuge in Him. Peter takes up the words to describe the believer’s growth: “as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: if so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.” The first taste of grace begets the appetite for more. The dictionary holds “taste and see” as the warm invitation of experiential religion: the goodness of God is not a doctrine to be admired at a distance but a reality to be proved in personal trust. It rebukes the merely notional believer who knows about God’s goodness yet has never tasted it, and it encourages the trembling sinner to come and prove for himself that those who trust the LORD are never put to shame.
webster_summary: The invitation of Psalm 34:8 to know God’s goodness by personal experience—to prove the LORD good by trusting Him—the warm heart of experiential religion.
webster_full: TASTE AND SEE, the invitation of Psalm 34:8 to know God’s goodness by experience.
“O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.”
To know God’s goodness not by report only but by personal proof.
Tasting is by trusting; the goodness is proved in taking refuge in Him.
Peter’s “if so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious” ties it to spiritual growth.
scriptures: Psa 34:8
O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.
How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!
corruption_summary: The call to experience God’s goodness is twisted into a religion of feelings divorced from His Word, or ignored by a merely notional faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the goodness of God is to be personally tasted, not merely admired at a distance. Many know the doctrine of God’s goodness who have never proved it in their own souls; the psalm summons them to come, trust, and taste for themselves. This is the warm heart of experiential religion: God’s goodness is a reality to be known by faith, not a fact to be filed away.

Yet the call to “taste” is corrupted when it is severed from God’s Word and made a pursuit of raw feeling or mystical experience. The same Scripture that bids us taste the LORD’s goodness bids us desire the sincere milk of the word, and the psalmist tastes God’s words sweeter than honey. The dictionary holds the two together: the goodness we taste is the goodness God reveals and promises in His Word, proved by trusting Him as He has spoken. The taste of grace is real and sweet, but it is the savoring of revealed truth, never a substitute for it.
roots_summary: The phrase invites the soul to prove God’s goodness by experience, tasting His grace through trust in His Word.
roots_lines: Hebrew tā’am — to taste, to perceive, to prove by experience.
Greek geuomai — to taste; “if so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.”
Tasting is bound to trusting: “blessed is the man that trusteth in him.”
The first taste of grace begets the appetite for the milk of the Word.
The figure marries personal experience to the revealed goodness of God.
usage: “Taste and see” is the classic invitation to experiential knowledge of God’s goodness.
It is preached to the notional believer who knows of God’s goodness but has not tasted it.
It is held to the Word against a pursuit of bare feeling or mystical experience.

etymology: From sound (whole, healthy) and mind; rendering Greek sōphronismos, self-control, sober-mindedness, given by the Spirit.
biblical_def: The sound mind is the Spirit-given gift of self-control, sober judgment, and disciplined thinking named by Paul: “For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.” The Greek word means more than mental health; it denotes self-mastery, sober-mindedness, a mind governed by truth rather than by passion or panic. Paul names it as one of three gifts the Spirit supplies in place of the spirit of fear, equipping the timid Timothy for bold and faithful ministry: power for the work, love for the people, and a sound mind to think clearly and act with disciplined self-control. Scripture everywhere calls the believer to this sober-mindedness—to gird up the loins of the mind, to be sober, to think on whatsoever things are true and honest and just and pure, and to be transformed by the renewing of the mind. The sound mind is the fruit of the Spirit’s sanctifying work upon the understanding: a mind brought under the authority of the Word, freed from the tyranny of fear and disordered desire, and made capable of sober, faithful, self-governed action. The dictionary holds the sound mind as a precious gift against an age of anxiety, intoxication, and unmastered passion: God’s people are not given over to fear or to the runaway emotions of the flesh, but are granted by the Spirit a disciplined, sober, self-controlled mind, ruled by truth and devoted to God.
webster_summary: The Spirit-given gift of self-control, sober judgment, and disciplined thinking—Paul’s “power, love, and a sound mind” replacing the spirit of fear.
webster_full: SOUND MIND, the Spirit-given gift of self-control and sober judgment.
“God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.”
The Greek means self-mastery and sober-mindedness, not merely mental health.
One of three gifts the Spirit supplies in place of fear, equipping for faithful service.
The fruit of the Spirit’s sanctifying work upon the understanding.
scriptures: For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
Wherefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ;
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
corruption_summary: “Sound mind” is reduced to mere mental wellness, severed from the Spirit’s gift of self-control and sober thinking under the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the sound mind is a gift of the Spirit, not merely a psychological state. The Greek word denotes self-mastery and sober-mindedness—a mind governed by truth and disciplined against fear and disordered passion. Against an age that prizes emotional intensity, anxiety, and unmastered desire, Scripture sets the believer’s calling to sober, self-controlled, truth-ruled thinking, supplied by God in place of the spirit of fear.

Where a corruption presses, it is the reduction of “sound mind” to mere mental wellness pursued by the techniques of the age, detached from the Word and the Spirit. The dictionary holds the fuller biblical sense: the mind is made sound as it is renewed by the Spirit, brought under the authority of Scripture, set on things true and pure, and freed from the tyranny of fear. The believer is not promised exemption from trouble, but is given a disciplined, sober mind to face it—power to act, love to serve, and self-control to think clearly in the fear of God.
roots_summary: The phrase names the Spirit-given discipline of the mind—self-control and sober judgment ruled by truth.
roots_lines: Greek sōphronismos — self-control, sober-mindedness, disciplined judgment.
Related to sōphrōn — sober, temperate, of sound mind, a required quality in elders.
Set against deilia — the “spirit of fear” or cowardice God has not given.
Paired with power (dunamis) and love (agapē) as the Spirit’s gifts.
The fruit of the renewed and Word-governed mind of Romans 12:2.
usage: The “sound mind” of 2 Timothy 1:7 is preached as the Spirit’s gift of self-control against fear.
It is taught as sober-mindedness, the mind renewed and ruled by Scripture.
It is distinguished from a merely psychological notion of mental wellness.
